summary: For ages 11–12: extend the order of operations to include an Indices tier (powers and roots) sitting between brackets and ×÷, and introduce the reciprocal as the multiplicative inverse (n × 1/n = 1, with ÷n = ×1/n). Learners evaluate complex expressions tier by tier, confront power-specific traps (2³ ≠ 2×3; −3² vs (−3)²; a root sign implies grouping), and grasp that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, not an arbitrary rule. Activities range from a live expression-resolving tool (primary proposal) through anchor charts, consolidation questions, and Socratic justification.
misconceptions: Evaluating powers as multiplication: 2³ = 6 instead of 8.
Applying the acronym literally — doing division before multiplication or addition before subtraction because I/D/A appear first.
Mishandling sign vs power: −3² taken as (−3)² = 9 rather than −(3²) = −9.
Thinking the reciprocal of n is −n (confusing multiplicative inverse with additive inverse) rather than 1/n.
Treating roots as outside the hierarchy, or evaluating under a root before resolving the bracket-like grouping the root implies (√(9+16) ≠ √9 + √16).

activities.title: Resolve the expression one tier at a time
steps: Work with a live expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and decide which operation to resolve next, following the hierarchy Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (left to right) → +− (left to right).
Resolve the power first: 2³ = 8 (write out 2×2×2 to confirm it is not 2×3 = 6), then ×4 = 32, then +3 = 35.
Deliberately try the wrong order — doing the addition before the multiplication: 3 + 2³ = 11, then × 4 = 44 — and compare 44 with the correct 35 so the two answers are seen to diverge.
Annotate an expression by shading each tier a different colour (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before collapsing it one tier per line: 3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35.
Evaluate √(9+16): resolve the grouping under the root first (9+16 = 25) then take √25 = 5, and check that this is not √9 + √16 = 3+4 = 7.
activities.insight: Indices (powers and roots) rank just below brackets and above ×÷; evaluating in the agreed order produces one unambiguous value, and a root implies grouping of what sits under it.

activities.title: The sign-versus-power boundary: −3² vs (−3)²
steps: Evaluate −3² by noting the power binds tighter than the negative sign: −3² = −(3²) = −9.
Evaluate (−3)² where the bracket groups the negative with the base: (−3)² = (−3)×(−3) = 9.
Add or remove a bracket around a negative number and predict how the value flips between −9 and 9 before confirming.
activities.insight: Without brackets, a power applies only to the number immediately beneath it, not to a preceding minus sign; bracketing changes what the exponent acts on.

activities.title: Reciprocals as multiplicative inverse
steps: State the reciprocal of a non-zero number n as 1/n and multiply n × 1/n, confirming the product is exactly 1 (e.g. 5 × 1/5 = 1); note that 0 has no reciprocal.
Compare dividing by n with multiplying by 1/n on the same number, checking the two operations give the same result (÷n = ×1/n).
Distinguish the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse, 1/n) from the negative (additive inverse, −n): the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5, not −5.
Match each number to its reciprocal (e.g. 4 ↔ 1/4, 2/3 ↔ 3/2).
activities.insight: Any non-zero number times its reciprocal is 1, so the reciprocal is what you multiply by to 'undo' multiplication, and dividing by a non-zero number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (0 has no reciprocal).

activities.title: Why do we need an agreed order? (justify the convention)
steps: Take a single expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and compute it under two different orders, recording the two different values (e.g. 35 vs 44).
Explain in your own words why mathematicians need one agreed order: so the same written expression communicates a single unambiguous value.
Respond to a prompt that offers two conflicting values and justify which order and result is correct and why.
activities.insight: The order of operations exists to remove ambiguity so notation communicates one value, not because any single order is inherently 'more correct'.

activities.title: Consolidation check
steps: Evaluate 3 + 2³ × 4 and justify why 35 is correct (not 44 from adding before multiplying, and not using 2³ = 6).
Decide whether −3² equals −9 or 9 and explain the bracket rule.
Match numbers to their reciprocals and state what each pair multiplies to.
activities.insight: Learners can evaluate expressions with the new tier correctly and articulate the reciprocal relationship under assessment conditions.

checkQuestion: Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4². Then tell me: why must everyone agree on an order for working this out — what would go wrong if they didn't?
checkAnswer: 50 (indices first: 4² = 16; then multiply: 3 × 16 = 48; then add: 2 + 48 = 50). The reason tier: without an agreed order the same expression would give different answers for different people, so the notation would be ambiguous and useless for communicating calculations.
